messages.content: I want to design a multipath transport that preserves reliable ordered delivery, bounded buffering, and bottleneck fairness during asymmetric path failures. The concrete requirements are to maintain delivery progress within 8 MiB of receiver buffering whenever at least one path remains usable, and to keep competing single-path flows’ throughput within 10% of their equal-share baseline at shared bottlenecks.

That sets a joint design objective. Data must still be delivered reliably and in order, delivery must continue with no more than 8 MiB of receiver buffering when at least one path remains usable, and the transport must not push competing single-path flows more than 10% away from their equal-share throughput baseline at shared bottlenecks. The asymmetric-failure setting matters because paths need not remain equally usable.
What does “asymmetric” contribute to the goal? I don’t want it to sound as though every path has to fail together.

It does not imply a simultaneous failure of all paths. The stated progress condition specifically covers the case in which at least one path remains usable despite trouble on another path. It does not prescribe a particular failure pattern, cause, or detection method.
And reliable ordered delivery is still required in that situation, not just some form of forward motion?

Yes. Progress cannot be obtained by abandoning the reliability or ordering requirement. Conceptually, if later data becomes available before earlier data, exposing it as though it were the next in-order data would not preserve ordered delivery. The goal is to keep delivery advancing while retaining that ordering and the 8 MiB receiver-buffering bound.
Could the receiver just stop delivering when its buffer reaches 8 MiB and call the buffering requirement satisfied?

Not if at least one path remains usable. Staying within 8 MiB addresses the buffer bound, but the same condition also calls for delivery progress. Indefinite lack of progress in that case would not satisfy both requirements merely because memory use stayed bounded.
Does the 8 MiB figure apply to all transport memory, or specifically to receiver buffering?

The stated numerical bound is specifically 8 MiB of receiver buffering. The node also calls for bounded buffering as a design property, but it gives no separate numerical limit for other storage. It would be inaccurate to present 8 MiB as an explicitly specified limit on every kind of transport memory.
What if no path remains usable? Is progress still part of this particular condition?

The explicit progress condition is qualified by “whenever at least one path remains usable.” It does not assert that delivery can advance when none is usable. That qualification does not remove the reliable ordered delivery objective; it defines when the stated progress guarantee applies.
I also want to be precise about fairness. Whose throughput is compared with the baseline?

It is the throughput of competing single-path flows at shared bottlenecks. Each such flow is compared with its equal-share baseline, with a permitted deviation of no more than 10%. The statement is not a requirement that the multipath transport’s own aggregate throughput be within 10% of that baseline.
Can you express that 10% comparison without assuming a particular link rate?

If a competing single-path flow’s equal-share baseline is B, then “within 10%” means its throughput is no less than 0.9B and no greater than 1.1B, using the baseline as the reference for the percentage. This expresses the comparison without assigning a numerical value to B or specifying how it is measured.
Why specify “at shared bottlenecks” rather than stating a general throughput target for every flow?

It identifies where the fairness comparison applies: where the multipath transport and competing single-path flows share a bottleneck. The requirement does not state a universal throughput target for flows on unrelated resources. Nor does it give a particular network configuration for calculating the equal-share baseline.
Does an asymmetric path failure make the fairness target optional while the transport tries to keep delivering?

No such exception is stated. The design goal brings reliable ordered delivery, bounded receiver buffering, delivery progress, and bottleneck fairness together during asymmetric path failures. Keeping delivery moving is not, by itself, grounds to set aside the specified 10% comparison for competing single-path flows at shared bottlenecks.
Conversely, could a design protect those single-path flows by letting its own ordered delivery remain stuck even though one path is usable?

That would address only one side of the goal. The stated requirement also calls for delivery progress within 8 MiB of receiver buffering whenever at least one path remains usable. Fairness and progress are concurrent constraints here, rather than alternatives from which the design may choose.
Does “delivery progress” specify a minimum rate or a deadline for delivering particular data?

No numerical progress rate or deadline is provided. The stated quantitative limits are the 8 MiB receiver-buffering bound and the 10% throughput deviation for competing single-path flows. Progress remains an explicit requirement, but assigning it a particular speed or time limit would add a specification that is not present.
And does “usable” have a numerical threshold in this goal?

No numerical threshold for path usability is specified. The condition is stated in terms of whether at least one path remains usable; it does not define usability by a particular capacity, delay, or other measurement. Those details should not be silently substituted for the stated condition.
How should I read the tension between ordering and the receiver-buffer limit, without presuming an implementation?

Ordered delivery constrains when data can be presented as the next data in sequence. If data becomes available out of order, that constraint can create pressure on receiver buffering; the requirement says the design must nevertheless maintain progress while staying within 8 MiB when a path is usable. This describes the problem the transport must solve, not a particular mechanism for solving it.

So the objective is not merely that a multipath connection survives an uneven failure. It must continue making ordered, reliable delivery progress within the receiver limit and remain fair to single-path competitors where they share bottlenecks?

Exactly. The design target is a multipath transport that preserves reliable ordered delivery and bounded buffering during asymmetric path failures, maintains delivery progress within 8 MiB of receiver buffering whenever at least one path remains usable, and keeps competing single-path flows’ throughput within 10% of their equal-share baseline at shared bottlenecks.
For the multipath transport, I propose DSN-based 8 MiB receive credits, gap-priority retransmission on healthy paths, and shared-bottleneck detection with aggregate TCP-fair congestion control.

Those are three complementary parts of a proposed design. DSN-based receive credits address how the receiver bounds the data it admits; prioritizing retransmission of gaps on healthy paths addresses interruptions to reliable ordered delivery; and shared-bottleneck detection with aggregate TCP-fair congestion control addresses the impact on competing flows. They are design choices aimed at the stated requirements, not proof by themselves that either numerical requirement is met.
What does DSN add to the receive-credit idea?

DSN means data sequence number. Referring to receive credits in terms of the data sequence gives the receiver a way to express its 8 MiB limit against the ordered data stream, rather than treating the paths as unrelated streams for this purpose. The proposal does not specify a credit encoding or a detailed accounting rule.
Is the 8 MiB credit figure the same 8 MiB from the receiver-buffering requirement?

Yes, the proposed 8 MiB receive credits are tied to that receiver-buffering limit. Their intended role is to prevent the transport from admitting data in a way that defeats the bound. The proposal alone does not establish that every possible source of receiver buffering is accounted for; that would need to be true for the design to meet the stated limit.
Why connect credits to the data sequence instead of just saying each path has an 8 MiB allowance?

The stated proposal is a DSN-based 8 MiB receive-credit scheme, not a separate 8 MiB allowance for each path. Conceptually, a limit tied to the overall ordered data stream addresses receiver buffering across the multipath transport. Giving each path its own independent 8 MiB allowance could describe a different limit, and it is not what this proposal states.
Could credits alone keep ordered delivery moving after an asymmetric path failure?

Credits address bounded admission, not the entire progress problem. Ordered delivery can be held up by missing earlier data even while later data is available. Gap-priority retransmission on healthy paths is the proposed complementary measure for that situation, while the credits keep receiver buffering bounded.
Explain “gap-priority retransmission” without assuming a particular packet format or scheduler.

A gap is missing data that matters to the data sequence. Giving its retransmission priority means addressing that missing data ahead of less urgent sending when the gap obstructs ordered delivery. The proposal says to retransmit on healthy paths; it does not specify packet formats, an exact ordering among multiple gaps, or a complete scheduling algorithm.
If later data has arrived, why emphasize the gap rather than that later data?

Because reliable ordered delivery cannot advance past missing earlier data merely because later data is present. Prioritizing a retransmission of the missing data is directed at the obstacle to in-order delivery. At the same time, the 8 MiB receive-credit limit is meant to constrain how much data can be held while delivery is obstructed.
Does “on healthy paths” mean that the failed or impaired path has to recover first?

No. The proposed response is to use healthy paths for gap-priority retransmission, rather than making recovery of the impaired path a prerequisite for retransmitting the missing data. The proposal does not define exactly how path health is determined.
The goal says progress whenever at least one path remains usable. Is “healthy” necessarily identical to “usable” here?

The two words are not explicitly defined as identical. The goal’s condition is that at least one path remains usable, while the proposal names healthy paths as the retransmission routes. To satisfy the goal, the design would have to preserve progress in the stated usable-path case; the proposal does not spell out how its path classification ensures that.
Is the retransmission priority a license to ignore the 8 MiB limit when an ordered gap is blocking delivery?

No. The proposal combines gap-priority retransmission with DSN-based 8 MiB receive credits. The retransmission is intended to help clear the obstacle to ordered delivery, while the credits are intended to keep receiver buffering within the limit. Treating one component as an exception to the other would not express the combined proposal.
And can the fairness component be set aside temporarily to make those retransmissions faster?

The proposal does not state such an exception. Its congestion-control component is aggregate TCP-fair control informed by shared-bottleneck detection. The design goal still includes keeping competing single-path flows’ throughput within 10% of their equal-share baseline at shared bottlenecks, even while addressing a delivery gap.
What is shared-bottleneck detection doing in the proposal?

It is intended to identify when paths contend at a shared bottleneck, so the transport can treat its congestion-control behavior there as an aggregate fairness matter. The proposal names detection but does not give a detection signal, an accuracy claim, or a specific response to uncertain classifications.
What does “aggregate TCP-fair” mean at that level of description?

It frames congestion control for the multipath transport collectively at a shared bottleneck, rather than treating each path as an unrestricted additional claim on the same resource. “TCP-fair” states the fairness aim; this proposal does not specify a congestion-control equation or a particular TCP variant. The numerical requirement remains the separate comparison against competing single-path flows’ equal-share throughput baseline.
So it would be too strong to say that merely detecting a shared bottleneck guarantees the competing flows stay within 10%?

Yes. Detection and aggregate TCP-fair congestion control are proposed means of pursuing that result, not a demonstrated guarantee. The 10% threshold is the requirement for competing single-path flows at shared bottlenecks; whether the proposed design actually keeps them within it is not established by the proposal alone.
Does the proposal say how to measure the equal-share baseline?

No. It retains the goal’s comparison to each competing single-path flow’s equal-share baseline but supplies no measurement procedure for that baseline. Adding a specific method here would go beyond the stated proposal.
How do the three pieces fit together when one path is impaired but another remains usable?

At a conceptual level, the DSN-based 8 MiB credits constrain receiver admission across the ordered data stream. If missing data blocks ordered delivery, gap-priority retransmission on healthy paths aims to address that blockage without depending on the impaired path. Shared-bottleneck detection and aggregate TCP-fair congestion control aim to keep that multipath activity fair where it competes with single-path flows. This explains their intended roles, not a claim that their unspecified details already meet the progress or 10% requirements.
Does this commit us to a fixed split of traffic across paths?

No fixed split is stated. The proposal specifies receive credits, a priority for retransmitting gaps on healthy paths, and a shared-bottleneck-aware aggregate congestion-control approach. It does not prescribe a general traffic split across paths.
Does it at least require the receiver to deliver data out of order so its buffer stays small?

No. Reliable ordered delivery remains part of the goal. The proposed gap-priority retransmission aims to resolve missing data that impedes that ordering, and the proposed credits aim to bound buffering while it is resolved. Neither component changes the delivery requirement to out-of-order delivery.
Can I describe this as a proposed decomposition of the design problem, rather than a finished transport?

Yes. It identifies mechanisms for three linked concerns: DSN-based 8 MiB receive credits for bounded receiver buffering, gap-priority retransmission on healthy paths for blocked ordered delivery, and shared-bottleneck detection with aggregate TCP-fair congestion control for fairness. The proposal does not supply the detailed rules or evidence needed to conclude that the transport already maintains delivery progress within 8 MiB whenever at least one path is usable or keeps competing single-path flows within 10% of their equal-share baseline.
How can the sender retransmit a failed path’s missing DSN after out-of-order data exhausts the 8 MiB receive window?

That is a potential progress problem for the proposed receive-credit scheme. If out-of-order data occupies the available 8 MiB and the missing DSN prevents ordered delivery, the receiver may be unable to free space by delivering the later data. If an exhausted window also prevents the sender from retransmitting the missing DSN, the two sides could remain stuck even though another path is usable. The proposal has not specified the credit rule needed to resolve that case.
So the issue is not simply whether a healthy path exists?

Right. A healthy path could carry a retransmission, but path availability alone does not say whether the sender is permitted to send it or whether the receiver can accept it within the 8 MiB buffering limit. The question is how those conditions interact when the receive window is exhausted.
Why can’t the receiver just deliver the out-of-order data to make room?

Because the goal requires ordered delivery. If that data follows the missing DSN, delivering it first would not preserve that ordering. The missing data is precisely what can prevent the receiver from releasing later data through in-order delivery.
Does “window exhausted” necessarily mean the missing DSN itself is outside the receiver’s advertised range?

Not necessarily. Exhaustion tells us that the available receive credit has been used, but the proposal has not defined how its DSN-based credits account for a missing position versus out-of-order data already received. That distinction matters: a rule that bars new data beyond a credited range need not have the same meaning as a rule that bars filling a gap within it. We cannot assume either rule is already part of the design.
Then is it safe to say retransmissions always bypass receive credits?

No. An unconditional bypass would be an additional protocol rule, and it could undermine the receiver-buffering bound if receiving a retransmission requires space that is not available. The question calls for a way to make the missing DSN deliverable without exceeding 8 MiB; it does not establish that every retransmission may ignore credits.
What exactly has to remain possible once later data fills the window?

The sender needs some way to retransmit the missing DSN on a usable path, and the receiver needs some way to accept the data needed to resume ordered delivery while keeping receiver buffering within 8 MiB. Otherwise, filling the window with later data could prevent the very retransmission that would unblock delivery. That states the required interaction, not a particular credit-accounting mechanism.
Could gap-priority retransmission solve it by itself?

Priority determines which data the sender tries to retransmit first; it does not, by itself, establish that an exhausted receive window permits the transmission or that the receiver has space for it. The proposed gap priority and the proposed 8 MiB credits have to be compatible for priority to help in this case.
Suppose the sender treats a zero-credit indication as a ban on every packet, including the missing DSN. What follows?

Under that hypothetical rule, the sender could not transmit the gap while the window is exhausted. If the receiver also cannot deliver the buffered later data until the gap arrives, there is no evident way for ordered delivery to advance merely by waiting for credit. That is the circular dependency your question exposes; it is not a claim that the proposed transport already uses that rule.
Does the 8 MiB requirement let us briefly exceed the limit to receive the missing data?

The stated requirement is to maintain delivery progress within 8 MiB of receiver buffering whenever at least one path remains usable. A proposed resolution should not depend on exceeding that stated receiver-buffering limit. The precise accounting that could make room for the missing data is not supplied here.
Is the missing DSN necessarily a large amount of data?

The question gives no size for the missing data. Its significance is its position in the ordered data sequence: even a gap whose size is unspecified can block delivery of data that follows it. We should not assume a particular packet size or amount of reserved space.
What if retransmitting it on the healthy path is possible from a congestion-control perspective?

That would address a different constraint, but it would not settle the receive-window question. The sender still needs a credit interpretation under which the retransmission can be sent and accepted within the buffer bound. Conversely, resolving receive credits would not remove the proposal’s aggregate TCP-fair congestion-control aim at shared bottlenecks.
So is the core ambiguity whether the 8 MiB credits limit new out-of-order arrivals, the gap retransmission, or both?

Yes. The proposal names DSN-based 8 MiB receive credits but does not specify what happens to retransmission eligibility when out-of-order data uses the available window. The crucial point is that credit exhaustion must not turn a missing DSN into an unfillable gap while a path remains usable, yet accepting it must not break the 8 MiB receiver-buffering bound.
Would it be accurate to present this as an unresolved design question rather than claim that the retransmission already works?

Yes. The question identifies an edge case the proposal must handle: out-of-order data exhausts the 8 MiB receive window, while the missing DSN from a failed path is needed for ordered delivery. Nothing stated so far specifies the credit-accounting rule that lets the sender retransmit that DSN on a usable path and the receiver accept it within the buffering limit.
Here’s a hypothesis for the exhausted-window case: a 64 KiB gap reserve and a 16 KiB maximum segment permit missing-DSN retransmissions after out-of-order credits close.

That hypothesis distinguishes the ability to accept data filling a missing DSN from permission to accept more out-of-order data. The 64 KiB reserve is intended to leave room for gap-filling retransmissions, while the 16 KiB maximum segment bounds the size of any one segment. It proposes a way for retransmission to remain possible after out-of-order credits close; it does not yet demonstrate that delivery will progress within the 8 MiB receiver-buffering limit.
Why specify both 64 KiB and 16 KiB? Wouldn’t a reserve alone express the idea?

The two figures play different roles. The 64 KiB figure describes the proposed gap reserve; the 16 KiB figure caps an individual segment that might use it. A reserve is more meaningful for this hypothesis if the data admitted to it has a bounded size. Those figures do not, on their own, define the full credit-accounting rule.
There’s a factor of four between them. Can I say the reserve holds four maximum-sized segments?

Arithmetically, 64 KiB equals four times 16 KiB. If the entire reserve were available and each segment occupied exactly its maximum size, four such segments would total 64 KiB. That arithmetic should not be turned into a guarantee that four retransmissions will always be accepted: the hypothesis does not specify what else might occupy the reserve or how its available space is tracked.
What exactly closes when out-of-order credits close?

In the hypothesis, it is permission to admit further out-of-order data under those credits. The proposed distinction is that closing those credits would not necessarily close the separate opportunity to receive retransmissions that fill missing DSNs. The exact signaling and eligibility rules for that distinction are not stated.
Is this the same as letting all retransmissions bypass the receive window?

No. The hypothesis names a finite 64 KiB gap reserve and a 16 KiB maximum segment. An unrestricted bypass for all retransmissions would be broader and could conflict with bounded receiver buffering. Here the proposed exception is specifically for missing-DSN retransmissions after out-of-order credits close, subject to the stated reserve and segment-size figures.
If out-of-order data has already used the entire 8 MiB of receiver buffering, where would the reserve fit?

That is an important accounting question for the hypothesis. To maintain progress within 8 MiB of receiver buffering, the 64 KiB reserve cannot simply be extra buffering on top of an already full 8 MiB. The hypothesis needs an interpretation under which room for gap data remains within the 8 MiB bound, but it does not specify the precise division or accounting of that space.
So “out-of-order credits close” need not mean every byte of the receiver’s 8 MiB is occupied by out-of-order data?

Correct. Under the proposed reserve idea, those credits could close while capacity intended for a missing-DSN retransmission remains. That is the conceptual distinction the hypothesis relies on. We should not infer a particular advertised-window value or exact credit calculation from it.
Why must the arriving data actually fill a gap? Would admitting some later retransmitted data be equivalent?

Not for the purpose stated here. The hypothesis concerns retransmissions of missing DSNs that can unblock reliable ordered delivery. A retransmission of later data that does not fill the obstructing gap would not necessarily make ordered delivery advance, while it could consume limited receiver space. The proposal does not specify a detailed test for qualifying retransmissions.
Does the 16 KiB maximum segment say how large the missing region can be?

No. It bounds a segment, not the total extent of a missing region. A missing region could require more than one retransmission; the hypothesis does not give a maximum gap size or guarantee that the 64 KiB reserve can accommodate every missing region at once.
If a gap needs more than 64 KiB to fill, does that refute the hypothesis immediately?

Not from the statement alone. The hypothesis says the reserve and segment limit permit missing-DSN retransmissions after out-of-order credits close; it does not say the entire gap must fit in the reserve simultaneously. Whether receiving some gap data permits in-order delivery and frees space for further retransmission depends on details not specified here. Nor can we assume that such advancement always occurs.
Would retransmitting the missing DSN still need a usable path?

Yes, in the context of the progress requirement, at least one path must remain usable. The reserve addresses a receiver-credit obstacle; it does not create a usable path or define how the sender chooses one. The hypothesis is about permitting a missing-DSN retransmission after out-of-order credits close, not about changing the path condition.
Is “permit” a claim that the sender has already succeeded in delivering the missing data?

No. It expresses the hypothesized possibility of sending and accepting the retransmission despite closed out-of-order credits. Actual delivery progress would also depend on the necessary retransmission occurring and the receiver being able to deliver data in order. No completed test or observed outcome is stated.
Does a gap reserve change the ordered-delivery requirement?

It does not. The purpose of reserving room for missing-DSN retransmissions is to support ordered delivery when later data is waiting behind a gap. It is not permission to present that later data out of order.
And does this hypothesis settle the competing-flow fairness requirement?

No. The 64 KiB gap reserve and 16 KiB maximum segment address receiver space and retransmission eligibility. They do not establish that competing single-path flows remain within 10% of their equal-share throughput baseline at shared bottlenecks. Retransmissions would still have to coexist with the proposed aggregate TCP-fair congestion control.
What is the narrowest accurate way to state what we think these two sizes accomplish?

The hypothesis is that keeping a 64 KiB gap reserve, together with a 16 KiB maximum segment, permits retransmission of missing DSNs even after credits for additional out-of-order data close. It identifies a possible way around the exhausted-credit obstacle while retaining the 8 MiB receiver-buffering objective; it does not by itself specify the accounting rules or prove progress and fairness guarantees.
To evaluate the gap-reserve hypothesis, let’s run ns-3 path-failure sweeps with saturated out-of-order credits, a 64 KiB gap reserve, and 16 KiB segments, and measure delivery stalls.

That is an evaluation activity, not a result. The ns-3 sweeps would examine path failures while credits for additional out-of-order data are saturated, using the stated 64 KiB gap reserve and 16 KiB segments. Measuring delivery stalls focuses the evaluation on whether ordered delivery gets stuck in the credit-exhaustion case the hypothesis is meant to address.
Why make the out-of-order credits saturated rather than leave them with room?

The hypothesis concerns missing-DSN retransmissions *after* out-of-order credits close. Saturating those credits puts the proposed reserve under that condition. If credits remained available, a lack of stalls would not directly answer whether the reserve helps once out-of-order admission has closed.
What does “path-failure sweeps” commit us to here?

It commits the activity to examining path-failure cases in ns-3 as a sweep, rather than describing a single observed run. The node does not specify the sweep’s parameters, failure timing, number of paths, or number of runs, so those should not be presented as already chosen.
Is the reserve being varied across the sweep?
That is not stated. The activity specifies a 64 KiB gap reserve for the sweeps. Calling it a sweep does not, by itself, mean that the reserve size is one of the variables being changed.
Likewise, should I describe a range of segment sizes?
No. The activity names 16 KiB segments. It does not specify a segment-size range or a comparison against other sizes.
What should count conceptually as a delivery stall, without inventing a numerical threshold?

The relevant observation is a pause in ordered delivery, particularly when missing data prevents later data from being delivered. Measuring stalls can reveal whether delivery remains blocked under the saturated-credit condition. The activity does not define a minimum pause duration, a reporting statistic, or a threshold for an acceptable stall.
Does measuring delivery stalls directly show that the sender could retransmit the missing DSN?

Not necessarily. Stall measurements address the observable progress question, but a stall or lack of one alone would not fully describe which retransmissions were permitted or how receive credits were accounted for. The stated activity is to measure delivery stalls; it does not specify additional instrumentation for identifying every internal cause.
Then why is this an evaluation of the reserve hypothesis at all?

Because the hypothesis proposes that the 64 KiB reserve, with the stated segment limit, permits missing-DSN retransmissions after out-of-order credits close. Delivery stalls during path failures are an observable consequence to examine when asking whether that proposed permission helps maintain ordered delivery progress. The activity is relevant to the hypothesis without predetermining what the measurements will show.
Should we say the sweeps have already shown that 64 KiB is enough?
No. The node says to run the ns-3 sweeps and measure stalls; it reports no runs or results. It also does not establish that 64 KiB suffices for every missing-data situation.
Does the phrase “saturated out-of-order credits” mean the entire receiver buffer must already be filled?

Not necessarily. It says the credits for additional out-of-order data are saturated. The proposed gap reserve is meant to distinguish that condition from having no room to accept missing data at all. The activity does not specify the detailed buffer accounting or an observed occupancy figure.
How does this relate to the 8 MiB receiver-buffering objective?

That objective motivates the credit and reserve problem: delivery should continue within 8 MiB of receiver buffering whenever at least one path remains usable. This activity specifically calls for measuring delivery stalls in the stated ns-3 sweeps. It does not report a buffering measurement or, by itself, demonstrate compliance with the 8 MiB bound.
And the single-path-flow fairness requirement—is it measured in this activity?

No fairness measurement is specified here. The activity measures delivery stalls under path failures with saturated out-of-order credits, a 64 KiB gap reserve, and 16 KiB segments. It should not be described as having measured competing single-path flows against their equal-share baseline.
So the accurate formulation stays narrow: run the simulation sweeps and observe whether ordered delivery stalls in this stressed credit state?

Yes. Run ns-3 path-failure sweeps with saturated out-of-order credits, a 64 KiB gap reserve, and 16 KiB segments, and measure delivery stalls. That evaluates the proposed gap-reserve behavior under the condition that motivated it, without asserting a result or adding unspecified sweep settings.
The ns-3 path-failure sweeps now have a result: in 1,000 failures with saturated out-of-order credits, ordered delivery resumed within 420 ms, and peak occupancy was ≤8 MiB.

That reports both an observed progress bound and an occupancy bound for those 1,000 simulated failures. Ordered delivery resumed within 420 ms despite the saturated out-of-order credits, and the reported peak occupancy did not exceed 8 MiB. Those are observations from the ns-3 sweeps, not a guarantee for every possible path failure.
Can I describe 420 ms as the average time to resume delivery?

No. “Resumed within 420 ms” gives an upper bound on the reported resumption time in those failures; it does not give an average or a distribution. We should not infer how many cases resumed much sooner.
Does it mean delivery never stalled?
No. Delivery could have paused and then resumed within 420 ms. The result reports resumption within that interval, not uninterrupted delivery or zero stall time.
What does the count of 1,000 tell us?

It tells us the stated observation covers 1,000 ns-3 failures with saturated out-of-order credits. It does not specify how those failures were distributed across path conditions, or establish behavior outside the simulated cases.
Should I say that every one of the 1,000 failures resumed within 420 ms?

That is the natural reading of “in 1,000 ns-3 failures ... ordered delivery resumed within 420 ms.” It is more precise than calling 420 ms an average. The statement does not identify the exact resumption time of any individual failure.
And is ≤8 MiB the receiver’s average occupancy?
No. It is a peak-occupancy statement: the reported peak was at most 8 MiB. An average cannot be calculated from that bound, and the result does not say how long occupancy remained near the peak.
Can we say peak occupancy was exactly 8 MiB?
No. The ≤ symbol allows a peak below 8 MiB as well as one equal to 8 MiB. The evidence gives a bound, not an exact peak value.
Remind me why saturated out-of-order credits are important to interpreting this result.

That condition puts the measurement in the stressed receive-credit situation at issue: additional out-of-order data cannot simply rely on spare out-of-order credits. The result says ordered delivery nevertheless resumed within 420 ms in the 1,000 simulated failures, with peak occupancy ≤8 MiB. It does not, by itself, specify the internal sequence of credit decisions or retransmissions in each case.
The sweeps used the 64 KiB gap reserve and 16 KiB segments. Can I attribute the observed resumption entirely to the reserve?

The reported result comes from sweeps with those stated settings, but it does not isolate the reserve’s contribution. Without additional information about what happened internally or a comparison condition, saying the reserve alone caused every resumption would go beyond the evidence. The observation is that delivery resumed within 420 ms under the reported setup.
Do the observations establish that a missing DSN was retransmitted in every failure?

They do not explicitly report individual retransmissions. Resumed ordered delivery is the reported outcome; the result does not enumerate missing DSNs, retransmission events, or the route each one took. Those details should not be presented as measurements from this result.
Does the result prove the transport will always make progress whenever one path remains usable?

No. It reports progress in 1,000 ns-3 failures under the saturated-credit condition. It does not state that every possible failure pattern or usable-path condition was represented, so it cannot be turned into a universal progress guarantee.
But within the reported failures, it is fair to say the delivery-progress and 8 MiB observations occurred together?

Yes. For the reported set, ordered delivery resumed within 420 ms and peak occupancy was ≤8 MiB. Keeping those observations together is useful: resumption was not reported as depending on a peak occupancy above the stated 8 MiB bound.
Does the 420 ms figure become a general deadline for the transport?

No. It is a measured bound in the stated ns-3 failures, not a newly specified deadline for all operation. The design goal requires delivery progress within the receiver-buffering limit when at least one path remains usable, but it does not set a universal 420 ms deadline.
Can I infer anything about competing single-path flows from these numbers?

No. Resumption time and peak occupancy do not report competing single-path flows’ throughput. This result does not say whether those flows were within 10% of their equal-share baseline at shared bottlenecks.
What would be a careful, compact statement of the evidence without overstating it?

In 1,000 ns-3 path failures with saturated out-of-order credits, ordered delivery resumed within 420 ms and peak occupancy was ≤8 MiB. That states the observed progress and occupancy bounds for the simulated failures without claiming an average, uninterrupted delivery, a particular retransmission mechanism in every case, or a fairness result.
Let’s adopt the 64 KiB gap reserve and 16 KiB segments. The reason for the decision is that ns-3 showed recovery within 420 ms and occupancy of ≤8 MiB.

The decision is to use those two settings together: a 64 KiB gap reserve and 16 KiB segments. Its stated basis is the ns-3 result—recovery within 420 ms while occupancy remained at or below 8 MiB. That supports adopting the settings without turning the observed bounds into guarantees for every future failure.
Should I describe this as a decision now, rather than another suggestion to consider?
Yes. “Adopt” makes the status of these settings clear. The gap reserve is 64 KiB and the segments are 16 KiB; the ns-3 recovery and occupancy observations are the stated reason for choosing them.
